question: A new model scores 92% on a well-known math benchmark but only 61% on a freshly written set of problems of the same difficulty. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The fresh set is badly written
The model is better at new problems than old ones
Contamination: the original test items likely appeared in training data, so part of the score is memorization
Math benchmarks are always saturated
explanation: A large gap between public items and fresh items of equal difficulty is the classic sign of contamination. Fresh or private test sets measure solving instead of recall.

question: Two models score 91.2% and 90.7% on a benchmark where frontier models have clustered above 90% for a year. What should you conclude?
options: Very little: the benchmark is saturated and the difference is within noise and label errors
The first model is clearly better for every task
The second model is cheaper
The benchmark has become harder
explanation: Saturated benchmarks stop separating models. Half a point near the ceiling says nothing about your use case.

question: A model leads an arena-style leaderboard built from human votes. Your task is extracting exact amounts from contracts. How should you weigh the rank?
options: As proof it is the most accurate extractor available
As irrelevant, because human votes are random
As a reason to skip evaluation
As evidence people prefer chatting with it; votes reward style, length and confidence, so test extraction accuracy on your own contracts
explanation: Arenas measure preference on the arena's prompts. Correctness on your specific task needs your own eval.

question: A launch table reports a model's coding score as "best of 8 attempts with a custom agent scaffold". Your product will call it once through the public API. What is the review comment?
options: The score applies directly to our setup
The reported setup differs from ours (attempts, scaffold); expect lower results and measure with our own single-call setup
Best-of-8 always lowers scores, so ours will be higher
Scaffolds are irrelevant to coding benchmarks
explanation: Number of attempts, prompting and tooling change scores a lot. Compare only numbers measured under the conditions you will run.

question: Which is the strongest basis for choosing between two shortlisted models for a ticket-classification feature?
options: Their average rank across five public leaderboards
The vendor's launch blog post
200 real tickets with known categories, run through both models with your prompt, measuring accuracy, cost and p95 latency
Which model is newer
explanation: A product eval uses your distribution and your scoring, cannot be contaminated by public data, and measures quality together with cost and latency. Module 10 builds it properly.
